title: Verbs that change form
goal: Tackle the biggest hurdle for English speakers: Portuguese verbs change their ending for every subject, not just *speak/speaks*. This unit sets up the first and largest group — verbs ending in **-ar**.
bekal: make negative sentences with *não* before the verb
drop the subject pronoun, because the verb ending already carries it

dialogs.title: Dialogue — O que você faz no fim de semana?
dialogs.intro: Friday afternoon, just before class ends. Carla and Budi chat about their routines.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.id: Budi, do you speak other languages?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Falo indonésio, inglês e um pouco de árabe.
lines.id: I speak Indonesian, English and a little Arabic.
lines.literal: I-speak Indonesian, English and a little of Arabic.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Nossa! E você estuda português todo dia?
lines.id: Wow! And do you study Portuguese every day?
lines.literal: gosh! and you you-study Portuguese every day?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Estudo de manhã. À noite eu trabalho.
lines.id: I study in the morning. At night I work.
lines.literal: I-study of morning. at-the night I I-work.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: At a Japanese restaurant. And you?

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.id: I don't work. I just study.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: E o que você faz no fim de semana?
lines.id: And what do you do on the weekend?
lines.literal: and what you you-do in-the end of week?

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Eu danço. Nós dançamos forró todo sábado.
lines.id: I dance. We dance forró every Saturday.
lines.literal: I I-dance. we we-dance forró every Saturday.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Que legal! Eu não danço nada.
lines.id: How cool! I don't dance at all.
lines.literal: what cool! I not I-dance nothing.

lines.speaker: Carla:
lines.text: Todo mundo dança no Brasil. A gente ensina você!
lines.id: Everybody dances in Brazil. We'll teach you!
lines.literal: all world it-dances in-the Brazil. we we-teach you!

notes: **This is the biggest difference from English.** English *speak* barely changes: I speak, you speak, she speak**s**. Portuguese changes the ending every time: *falo*, *fala*, *falamos*, *falam*. The good news: only **the ending** changes — the stem (*fal-*) stays intact forever.

**Because the ending already carries the subject, the pronoun can be dropped.** Look at Budi's answer: *Falo indonésio*, not *Eu falo indonésio*. The ending *-o* can only mean "I". Brazilians drop it all the time, especially *eu*. Use *eu* when you want to **stress** or contrast: *Eu não trabalho, ela trabalha*.
**Não goes right before the verb.** *Eu não trabalho.* Just one word, always in the same spot, with no helper verb. That's much simpler than English *I don't work* — no *do*, no *does*.

⚠️ **The double negative is correct.** *Eu não danço nada* is literally "I don't dance nothing" — two negatives in one sentence, and it's **required**. The same goes for *não tem ninguém* (there's nobody) and *não vou nunca* (I'll never go). Leaving out *não* is what's wrong. Forget what your English teacher told you.

**Todo mundo** literally means "all the world", but it means "everybody", and it takes the **singular** verb: *todo mundo dança*. It's one of the most common expressions in Brazil, and the formal *todos* actually sounds stiff in conversation.

grammars.title: -ar verbs: the biggest group
body: About eighty percent of Portuguese verbs end in **-ar**, and almost all are regular. Remove *-ar* from the infinitive, then add the endings below.
after: ⚠️ Look at the pronunciation in row four: **-am** at the end of a verb is said **own**, just like *-ão*. So *falam* sounds like FAH-lown, and *trabalham* like trah-BAH-lyown. It's one of the sounds beginners mispronounce most.

**Row five is the biggest shortcut in spoken Brazilian Portuguese.** Since *a gente* uses the same form as *ele*, you can talk all day with just **three** forms: *-o* for I, *-a* for everyone else in the singular including *a gente*, and *-am* for the plural. The *-amos* form can wait.

**The endings -o and -a have nothing to do with gender here.** This confusion often pops up after unit 2: *eu falo* uses *-o* whether the speaker is a man or a woman. Verb endings mark **the subject**, adjective endings mark **gender** — two systems that happen to use the same letters.

grammars.title: The twenty most common -ar verbs
body: All regular. Once you know the endings, these twenty verbs are ready to use in five forms each.
after: ⚠️ Two verbs in that table hide a small **spelling** change that only shows up later in the past tense, purely to keep the sound: *chegar* → *cheguei* (a *u* is added so the g stays hard) and *dançar* → *dancei* (ç becomes c before e). In the present tense, both are fully regular.

**Achar is the most typically Brazilian verb.** It means "to think, to reckon" — *Eu acho que sim* ("I think so"), *O que você acha?* ("What do you think?"). It's used far more than *pensar*, and mastering it makes your conversation sound natural right away.

grammars.title: Gostar de — to like, with a required little word
body: One verb that needs special attention, because its form is a trap.
after: ⚠️ **De can't be dropped.** *Eu gosto café* is wrong, and it's one of the mistakes that survives longest, into the intermediate level. Think of *gostar de* as one whole unit, like "to be fond of" — and never split it.
And since *de* meets the article, it merges just like in unit 5: *gosto **do** Brasil*, *gosto **da** música*, *gosto **dos** livros*.

blocks.text: These time expressions attach to almost any verb sentence, and you can use all of them right now.
⚠️ *Nunca* triggers a double negative when it comes after the verb: *Eu não danço nunca*. When it comes before, *não* is dropped: *Eu nunca danço*. Both are correct and mean the same thing.
Portuguese names the weekdays by **number** — a quirk no other major European language shares, and one that makes them easy to learn.
In conversation, the *-feira* part is almost always dropped: people say *segunda*, *terça*, *quinta*. Notice also that the count starts at **two**, because Sunday counts as the first day.

To say "on Monday", add the article: *na segunda* (this Monday) and *às segundas* (every Monday, on Mondays). The five weekdays are feminine; *sábado* and *domingo* are masculine — so *no sábado*, *no domingo*.

I'm twenty-five years old → *Eu tenho vinte e cinco anos*
There are twelve students → *Tem doze alunos*
Four hundred reais a month → *quatrocentos reais por mês*
